title: How a somite splits

objective.text: Trace how a somite divides and what each of its parts goes on to build.

body.general: How does one block build bone, muscle and skin? Each somite starts as a ball of cells that becomes a hollow ring [f1]. Early in week 4, cells of its lower inner wall loosen and wrap around the neural tube (future spinal cord) [f2]. This part, the sclerotome, makes vertebrae and ribs [f3]. The rest, the dermomyotome, holds muscle-forming cells and the dermatome [f4,f5]. The dermatome forms the deep skin (dermis) of the back [f4]. The dermomyotome builds the back and body-wall muscles [f6]. Some cells travel out to form most limb muscles [f7].
body.mbbs: A new somite is a ball of paraxial mesoderm that becomes an epithelial ring around a small cavity [f1]. Early in week 4 its ventral and medial wall loosens and migrates around the neural tube and notochord [f2]. This sclerotome forms the vertebrae and ribs [f3]. Cells at the dorsomedial and ventrolateral edges are muscle precursors; the cells between them are the dermatome [f4]. Together these make up the dermomyotome [f5]. It forms the dermis of the back and the muscles of the back and body wall [f6]. Ventrolateral cells also migrate into the body wall and limbs, giving the obliques, transversus abdominis and most limb muscles [f7]. Each somite keeps its own segmental nerve wherever its cells go [f8].

facts.text: A new somite is a ball of mesoderm that becomes an epithelial ring around a small cavity.
Early in week 4, the somite's ventral and medial wall loosens and moves around the neural tube and notochord.
These loosened cells are the sclerotome, which forms the vertebrae and ribs.
Cells at the dorsomedial and ventrolateral edges of the somite are muscle precursors; the cells between, the dermatome, form the dermis of the back.
The muscle precursors and the dermatome together form the dermomyotome.
The dermomyotome forms the dermis of the back and the muscles of the back and body wall.
Ventrolateral cells also migrate into the body wall and limbs, forming the obliques, transversus abdominis and most limb muscles.
Each somite keeps its own segmental nerve wherever its cells go.
SHH and noggin from the notochord and neural-tube floor plate switch on PAX1 and make sclerotome.
WNT from the dorsal neural tube gives PAX3 dermomyotome and MYF5 muscle cells; BMP4, FGF and epidermal WNT give MYOD muscle precursors; NT-3 gives dermis.

misconceptions.right: The dermatome forms the dermis (deep skin); the epidermis (outer skin) comes from ectoderm (the top germ layer).
Limb bones and connective tissue come from the lateral plate (the outer strip of middle-layer tissue); only limb muscles come from somites.

misconceptions.wrong: Each somite simply becomes one vertebra.
misconceptions.right: The sclerotome gives vertebrae and ribs, while the dermomyotome gives muscle and dermis.

checks.why: The dermatome gives the dermis, the deeper skin layer; the epidermis on top comes from ectoderm (the top germ layer).

checks.prompt: What do somite cells contribute to the limbs?
checks.why: Somite cells migrate in as limb muscle; bones and connective tissue come from the lateral plate (the outer strip of middle-layer tissue).

checks.prompt: Put these steps of somite change in order.
options: A solid ball of cells forms
The cells form a hollow ring
Cells wrap around the neural tube
checks.why: The ball first becomes a hollow ring; in week 4 its lower inner wall loosens, and those cells wrap the neural tube.

adult: Sclerotome becomes vertebrae and ribs [f3]; dermomyotome becomes back dermis and the muscles of the back, body wall and limbs [f6,f7].

remember.a: The dermis (deep skin layer) of the back [f4].

remember.q: When a somite's cells move away, what happens to their nerve supply?
remember.a: They keep their own nerve, from their body segment, wherever they go [f8].
